questions.text: For an LEA item on roof rainwater drainage, what is the best source-safe sizing basis under the checked RNPC family?

options.text: Use maximum rainfall intensity together with the roof area served.
Size every roof drain only by the number of occupants.
Treat rainwater pipe sizing as the same calculation as fixture-unit sanitary drainage.
Use a product brochure as the controlling sizing rule.

questions.rationale: The RNPC rainwater section sizes storm drainage by rainfall intensity and roof area, with local rainfall intensity used for the locality.
questions.explanation: A confuses the coefficient with the area parameter (A). Confuses C with the intensity parameter (I), which has units mm/hr. Confuses the Rational Method formula with cistern volume equations; Q is discharge, not storage. C is the runoff coefficient, accounting for infiltration, evaporation, and surface retention. It is always ≤ 1. Concrete roofs have C ≈ 0.85; gravel-covered roofs have C ≈ 0.55 (standard hydrology tables per engineering practice).
questions.code_citation: Revised National Plumbing Code of the Philippines; Linsley, Kohler & Paulhus

questions.text: Which coordination rule best protects the sanitary system when handling roof rainwater?

options.text: Keep rainwater piping separate from soil, waste, and vent piping.
Route roof rainwater into the nearest soil stack by default.
Use sanitary vent piping as the overflow path for roof drains.
Ignore drainage separation once a pipe is concealed.

questions.rationale: The checked RNPC family states that rainwater piping is not used as soil, waste, or vent piping and restricts rain/surface water discharge to excreta drainage systems.
questions.code_citation: Philippine National Electrical Code; Building Code for the Philippines (PD 1096)

questions.text: What should an architect remember about roof drain strainers under the checked RNPC family?

options.text: The strainer net inlet area should be at least equal to the outlet area it serves.
A strainer may reduce inlet area below the outlet area when aesthetics require it.
Strainers are not part of storm drainage coordination.
The strainer rule applies only to sanitary floor drains.

questions.rationale: The checked RNPC roof-drain provisions require a strainer with adequate net inlet area in relation to the outlet.
questions.code_citation: PAGASA climatic data; Green Building Code (RA 9729 IRR); PD 1096 Building Code

questions.text: Which slope statement is source-safe for horizontal drainage piping under the checked RNPC family?

options.text: Horizontal drainage piping generally uses at least 20 mm per meter, with limited approval for 10 mm per meter on 102 mm and larger pipe.
Horizontal drainage piping may be installed level when hidden above a ceiling.
Slope is selected only after construction, based on available ceiling space.
Rainwater piping has no need for grade because it is not sanitary piping.

questions.rationale: The checked RNPC slope provision gives 20 mm per meter as the general minimum and allows 10 mm per meter for 102 mm and larger piping only with approval.

questions.text: A mixed-use development (1.8 hectares total, comprising 50% rooftop area with C = 0.85, 30% paved parking with C = 0.90, and 20% landscaped areas with C = 0.25) experiences a 10-year storm with intensity 140 mm/hr (per PD 1096 for the region). The developer proposes a 200 mm diameter storm drain at 0.75% slope (capacity ~0.050 m3/s per code tables). Will this pipe be sufficient, and why or why not?

options.text: No. The calculated discharge is approximately 0.522 m3/s, exceeding the pipe capacity of 0.050 m3/s by a factor of 10; a much larger diameter (450 mm or higher) is required.
Yes. The design discharge is less than 0.050 m3/s, so the 200 mm pipe is adequate and economical.
No. The landscape area has C = 0.25, which reduces total runoff below 0.050 m3/s; but water quality standards require a 300 mm pipe regardless.
Yes. Since this is a mixed-use site with some infiltration, the average coefficient is less than 0.60; the 200 mm pipe exceeds minimum requirements.

questions.rationale: Step 1 - Weighted runoff coefficient (area-weighted): C = (0.50 x 0.85) + (0.30 x 0.90) + (0.20 x 0.25) = 0.425 + 0.27 + 0.05 = 0.745. Step 2 - Rational Method with SI conversion constant: Q (m3/s) = 0.00278 x C x I (mm/hr) x A (ha) = 0.00278 x 0.745 x 140 x 1.8 = 0.522 m3/s. Step 3 - Compare to pipe capacity: 0.522 m3/s vs 0.050 m3/s = factor of 10.4 exceedance. The 200 mm pipe is grossly undersized; correct answer is a. The original option a value of 0.0724 m3/s resulted from using C = 0.103 (erroneous: it appears the area fractions were multiplied twice or the landscaped C=0.25 dominated the weighting). Option b and d are incorrect because the weighted C of 0.745 is above 0.60 (not below). Option c is incorrect because the landscaped fraction (20%) is too small to reduce total runoff below 0.050 m3/s.
questions.code_citation: PD 1096 Building Code; Revised National Plumbing Code of the Philippines; Rational Method Application

questions.text: A storm drain must accommodate a peak discharge of 0.120 m3/s. The rainfall intensity for the design storm is 160 mm/hr, and the runoff coefficient for the catchment is 0.72. What is the minimum drainage area (in hectares) that this discharge represents under the Rational Method?

options.text: 0.0375 hectares
0.375 hectares
3.4 hectares
37.5 hectares

questions.rationale: Rational Method in SI units: Q (m3/s) = 0.00278 x C x I (mm/hr) x A (ha), where 0.00278 = 1/3600 x (1 m / 1000 mm) x (10000 m2 / 1 ha). Solving for area: A = Q / (0.00278 x C x I) = 0.120 / (0.00278 x 0.72 x 160) = 0.120 / 0.3201 = 0.375 ha. Correct answer is b. Option a (0.0375 ha) results from a decimal-place error. Option c (3.4 ha) is the original erroneous marked answer (off by a factor of ~9; would imply Q = 1.09 m3/s, not the 0.120 m3/s given in the stem) and reflects omission of the 0.00278 SI conversion constant. Option d (37.5 ha) results from dividing by 0.00278 twice.
questions.code_citation: PD 1096 Building Code for the Philippines; Rational Method

questions.text: A drainage catchment of 3.2 hectares experiences a peak rainfall intensity of 150 mm/hr. The runoff coefficient for mixed residential development is 0.68 (standard hydrology tables). Mixed development runoff coefficient is 0.60-0.75 (standard tables). Calculate the peak discharge using the Rational Method.

options.text: 0.0907 m3/s (approx 91 L/s)
0.454 m3/s (approx 454 L/s)
0.907 m3/s (approx 907 L/s)
3.264 m3/s (approx 3264 L/s)

questions.rationale: Rational Method in SI units: Q (m3/s) = 0.00278 x C x I (mm/hr) x A (ha), where 0.00278 = 1/3600 x (1 m / 1000 mm) x (10000 m2 / 1 ha). Substituting: Q = 0.00278 x 0.68 x 150 x 3.2 = 0.907 m3/s (approximately 907 L/s). Correct answer is c. Option a (0.0907 m3/s) results from a decimal-place error. Option b (0.454 m3/s) would correspond to an intensity of 75 mm/hr (half the stated value). Option d (3.264 m3/s) results from omitting the 0.00278 SI conversion constant (computing Q = C x I x A directly = 0.68 x 150 x 3.2 = 326.4, then dividing by 100). The original marked answer b (0.136 m3/s) was off by a factor of approximately 6.7.
questions.code_citation: PD 1096 Building Code for the Philippines; Linsley, Kohler & Paulhus
